section.title: A learning project becomes a community of engineering stories
section.deck: Ryan Peterman explains how the podcast grew from deliberate speaking practice into a way to surface engineers whose work is better known inside companies than outside them.

blocks.question: Why create a podcast about senior engineers’ careers?
answer: Ryan wanted to become a better speaker, a skill he believes affects careers, relationships, and how others perceive someone. Toastmasters supplied useful practice, but he found that recordings often went unreviewed amid other priorities. Publishing created a stronger commitment: because people would listen, he examined every word during editing. The content became both practice and a feedback loop.

He chose an initially modest goal of one episode per month because he already had substantial responsibilities. The process turned out to be enjoyable in its own right: he could have conversations he wanted to have with engineers he admired. Internal Facebook career narratives had earlier absorbed him with their accounts of impressive work and growth. The podcast sought to bring those otherwise little-known stories to a wider industry audience.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: What surprised you behind the scenes of successful episodes?
answer: Ryan remembers being unusually absorbed while recording with Philip Su, whose writing he had admired inside Meta. Strong engagement during the conversation and rapid audience growth afterward suggested that other engineers valued these career stories too. He felt similar energy with Ethan Evans and especially admired the guest’s ability to speak clearly.

Trailers created a separate challenge. Established shows can rely on reputation, but a new show may need to explain quickly why an unfamiliar guest is worth hearing. An especially aggressive trailer thrilled him at first, then audience feedback pushed him to balance attention-grabbing excerpts with taste and ease of listening. He considers shorter or absent trailers for recurring audio-podcast listeners while keeping a carefully edited introduction for discovery on YouTube. These are his plans at the time, rather than a promise about the current distribution format.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: Which future guests are you trying to find?
answer: His ideal guests are highly accomplished engineers known within their company or organization but not necessarily famous publicly. They may have substantial technical and career stories without being active on social media. Standard searches do not reliably reveal that group.

His own big-tech network supplied early guests. Audience recommendations then became a way to find admired senior ICs at other companies. He describes viewers’ suggestions leading to planned conversations at Apple, Google, and Microsoft. The sourcing challenge explains why community participation matters to the show’s editorial direction.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: What was harder about podcasting than ordinary conversation?
answer: Natural verbal acknowledgments—short agreements and listening noises—can obscure a guest’s answer in an audio recording. Ryan had to learn to express engagement with nods while holding back interruptions. Producing something pleasant to hear calls for a different listening habit than an unrecorded conversation.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Peterman

blocks.question: How do you balance a full-time engineering job with publishing?
answer: He finds it difficult and rejects an effortless side-project picture. For roughly two years he often stayed up until about four in the morning on Thursdays to finish a newsletter. A fellow newsletter writer cautioned him about burning the candle at both ends, and experience convinced him the warning was justified.

Content work pushes out other parts of life when meeting the day job’s expectations already takes substantial effort. He believes additional family or time commitments would have made the arrangement much harder. The account is an honest cost description, not a recommended sustainable schedule.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Peterman
